messages:
maria: Quick check-in — thinking about a different approach to reduce fragmentation: instead of frequent micro-evictions we could run periodic virtual-heap compaction that migrates live pages within host-backed staging and coalesce small free runs.
aj: sounds heavy. what's the compaction trigger? CPU bound? memory-pressure? :thinking_face:
maria: plan: trigger on two conditions: (1) host staging fragmentation > 25% over sliding 10m window, (2) eviction rate rising and tail latency > 95th SLO. compaction runs asynchronously on background threads, throttled by per-GPU CPU budget.
samir: migration across GPUs? cross-node moves? that's going to be expensive for large KV cache.
maria: not cross-node for now. compaction stays local to the node. it re-lays out the virtual heap: move live pages to create larger contiguous free ranges, update mappings. should reduce small-page churn and allocation failures.
liam: question: how do we coordinate with existing evictor? compaction could fight the evictor and make churn worse.
maria: evictor policy would switch to 'passive' during compaction window for affected arenas. idea: evictor marks ranges as "compacting" and skips them; compaction owns placement for a few seconds.
aj: what's the rollback plan if compaction stalls? we can't block allocations for long.
maria: compaction must be preemptible and staged. Each stage has a small per-stage deadline (e.g., 50ms) and we checkpoint progress. Allocator still services allocations from a fallback pool (coarse-grain slab) when a range is locked.
samir: fallback pool growth could increase fragmentation by itself.
liam: can we simulate this workload with the 250-token chat traces? run stress with short bursts and measure failure rate.
infra-bot: perf-run #6578 started: compaction-vs-evictor sim, scale=32, duration=30m, seed=20260320-1
aj: initial concerns: CPU cost and write amplification — we're moving pages that might be re-referenced immediately.
maria: agree. hence compaction only for pages with low recency score (LRU-age > threshold) and with eviction history. we avoid moving hot pages.
aj: what about NVMe staging? migrating pages will touch host staging I/O; could thrash NVMe.
liam: maybe couple compaction with an I/O budget and slow down when NVMe queue depth > 128.
samir: also need to consider multiprocess contention: multiple models pulling memory can cause compaction to thrash across arenas. We should area-tag compaction to tenant/gpu/engine.
maria: yes, compaction scoped to an allocator shard and tenant tag. config knobs: compaction_enabled, max_cpu_ms_per_minute, nvme_qd_limit, recency_age_ms.
devex: i put a short doc draft here: https://redwood.internal/devex/compaction-proposal — pls add comments.
aj: can we get a rough perf hypothesis? i expect lower allocation failures and lower 95th lat but +10-30% CPU.
maria: hypothesis: at 20-30% fragmentation, compaction reduces allocation retries by ~60% and 95th latency by ~15% for small-alloc workloads; overall CPU cost ~+18%.
liam: sounds acceptable if we gate by fragmentation metric and auto-disable when cost > threshold.
samir: one more: need correctness proofs for mapping updates — race between compaction move and request reading old mapping. use sequence numbers and atomic swap of page descriptors + TLB shootdown where necessary.
maria: implementation note: we plan to use versioned descriptors and a lightweight epoch mechanism to guarantee readers see either old or new mapping. TLB flush only when crossing physical address spaces.
aj: ok can you open RFC follow-up with code sketch for the epoch and compaction stages? I'll take perf harness.
maria: will do. starting a draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8423
devex: tagging @all for visibility. please react with :eyes: when you reviewed.
liam: :eyes:
aj: :+1:
samir: :+1:
